blocks.text: The destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE is the most probable historical setting for this poem, although its exact date is not stated. The chapter speaks of the Lord as acting “like an enemy” while also naming human enemies. It presents “daughter Zion” as Jerusalem personified: a bereaved city who is also figured as a mother, sufferer, and speaking complainant. The repeated attention to children fainting from hunger, including the horror voiced in verses 20–22, makes starvation and maternal loss central to the poem’s accusation.

Lamentations is received as five poems, each with its own voice and formal profile. Chapters 1–4 use alphabetic structures, while chapter 5 has twenty-two lines without the same alphabetic progression. This places chapter 2 within a carefully shaped collection of poems rather than as an isolated lament.
